fallacies.location: The Coronation of King Charles will be the first time in 70 years that the UK or even the world has seen such a historic spectacle.
fallacies.explanation: The statement implies the significance of the event based on its historical precedent rather than providing current relevance or necessity.

fallacies.location: It is the first time in recent history that an already existing crown will be used during the Coronation of a Queen Consort instead of a new one being made.
fallacies.explanation: The mention of using an old crown instead of making a new one appeals to tradition without addressing whether this is the best or most practical choice.

fallacies.location: Dr Tessa Dunlop previously told the Mirror: 'History suggests working royals will stand out.'
fallacies.explanation: The argument relies on Dr. Tessa Dunlop's authority and historical context without providing concrete evidence or reasoning for why this should be the case.

fallacies.location: Like it or not this state occasion is all about royal hierarchy.
fallacies.explanation: The statement presents a false dilemma by suggesting that the event can only be about royal hierarchy, ignoring any other possible interpretations or purposes.

fallacies.location: If you look at the footage of the 1953 Coronation, who was very prominent, albeit briefly? Prince Charles. He was four.
fallacies.explanation: Invoking the precedent of Prince Charles's prominence at the 1953 Coronation as a reason for inviting Archie relies on tradition rather than current circumstances or reasoning.
